old: Read this slowly into a recorder, speak it aloud, or learn its movement and use silent words if that comes easily. Choose one anchor—a sound, bodily contact, or your two-hand practice—and an opening phrase. Keep using the same anchor where the words refer to it. Pause between paragraphs; don’t read the delivery directions aloud.
Let your eyes settle somewhere in the room, somewhere they can rest for a little while, and notice the difference between looking for something and letting what is already there come into view.

There is a surface beneath you. Notice where you meet it … the contact, the pressure, whatever you can actually feel. And while you notice that, a sound may reach you, or a breath may draw your attention, without needing you to arrange either one.
You can give this a little time.

A thought about the day may still be here. A thought about whether you’re doing this properly may be here too. There is room to notice a thought and return to the anchor you chose, without finishing the thought first.

And as you return, you may find one detail that holds your interest … something about the sound, or the contact, or that particular way of listening … and let attention stay with it long enough to become curious.

Perhaps you can give yourself the time you would give someone you care about who has begun to speak and hasn’t yet found the words. You can remain nearby, listening, without finishing their sentence for them.
Let your chosen phrase come to mind now. Say it as an invitation, and notice how it is received.
As you continue, your eyes can close, soften, or stay open. Let that be a choice you make. Listening may deepen while a sound from the room remains available in the background.
Count slowly from five to one. Give each number its own moment.

Five. Notice your chosen anchor again. Four. Let attention gather around what you find. Three. Leave a little space after the words. Two. Listen into that space, without preparing an answer. One. Stay here for a moment.
Bring your chosen concern lightly to mind, or remain with your wish for contact. Let it be present without rehearsing its whole story.
What am I noticing now?
Give the response time to take its own form. It might be a sensation, a few words, an image, a feeling, or an impulse to move. There may be nothing clear yet.
Leave room to notice, with words or without them.
new: Guided Meditation: How to Listen These instructions are for use after you've read the chapter on Listening . It's best to practisise reading it slowly into a recorder, or read it aloud or if you're a pro even learn it and just say the words silently. Choose one of the three anchors to use, and read the instructions using that as 'the anchor' throughout. Also choose one of the opening phrases to use. At the end of each paragraph pause for a few moments. Don't read out loud the instructions for how to read it.
Let your eyes rest for a moment somewhere in the room.
As you do that, notice the surface that you are on, and how it feels to be in contact with it. As you do that, notice how even a sound, or a breath can bring your attention.
Remember that you have all the time in the world to do this.
Even if your attention is on a thought from the day, or even a thought about how you should be doing this, can you bring your attention back to your anchor even if there is a thought there?
In fact, notice one aspect of listening to the sound or being in contact or whatever you are doing to bring your attention which is interesting to you.
Remember that you can take as long to do this as you would give to a loved one if they were talking to you.
Now say to yourself (the opening phrase you've chosen) and notice how you receive that.
You can close your eyes or soften them or proceed with them open as you prefer. Notice how the listening opens up now, but perhaps you can still use the sound in the room in the back ground.
Now slowly count to yourself from 5 down to 1.
5 (notice your chosen anchor once more) 4 3 2 1
Bring to mind your chosen concern, or even just the wish to come into contact.
Now, what do you notice?
Take your time to notice what comes to you, whether it's sensations, words, images, feelings, urges to do something or even nothing at all.
Take your time to notice this, with or without words.
Working when you've already opened a state Before you try to deepen a state it's useful to contain it first.

old: Use this when loveyhuasca, meditation, lucid dreaming, grief, music, prayer, erotic energy, exhaustion, or intense beauty has already opened the state. Stabilize before making it stronger.
“The state is already open. I do not need to intensify it. I need to aim it, stabilize it, and keep it kind.”

Look around the room. Name where you are. Name the date, or at least the day. Feel your feet, hands, and spine. Press your thumbs gently but firmly against your index fingers. Focus on the physical friction of skin meeting skin.
“Only what can be integrated is welcome now. Anything too much can wait. The body may stay safe. The adult self remains present. The inner child does not have to carry this alone.”
Once you’re oriented, choose one intention:
“Please show me the next useful truth, symbol, feeling, question, or action — only in the amount I can live well with.”
new: This is useful when you've already opened a state, through means other than doing a deliberate process - like taking loveyhuasca, doing a different style of meditation, being in a lucid dream, dealing with grief, listening to music, praying, engaging with erotic energy, exhaustion or even being overwhelmed by the beauty of something. When you've done that, then you want to stabilize the state before making it stronger.
Say to yourself 'The state is already open, now I just need to aim it, stabilize it and be kind to myself as I do.'

Look around you in the room, notice where you are and what date (or at least what day) it is. Feel your feet, hands and spine to ground yourself. Focus on the physical sensation of pressing your thumbs against your index fingers, feel the friction.
Say to yourself 'I will only allow myself to go as far as I can integrate. If there is more, it can wait. My body will be safe, my adult self will be present as my inner child deals with this.
Once you are oriented, then pick one of the following: 'Please show me the next thing I need to know, in a form (symbol, feeling, question, action) that I can integrate.'

old: Sit upright. Open the eyes. Feel the feet. Let the breath be natural.
Say: “I am not going away. I am coming more fully here.”
Look at one object. Feel the spine.
“Is this daydream guidance, emotional digestion, or avoidance?”
“If it is guidance, show me the action inside it. If it is avoidance, bring me gently into the present and show me what I am avoiding.”

If stillness makes you sleepy, diffuse, or escape-prone, hypnosis can become more alert rather than more relaxed. Keep the eyes open and pair a small repeated hand movement with increasing clarity; stop the movement and notice what remains without trying to disappear inward.

“Eyes open. Press thumb and forefinger together gently. Release. Again — clearer, not sleepier. One more time. Now stop the deliberate movement. Notice the first second after the rhythm ends. Is there an echo in the fingers, the breath, the attention, or nowhere at all? Stay upright and work from exactly that level of alertness.”
new: Staying awake when your mind wants to escape You can do this sitting up, with your eyes open, feeling your feet, and allowing your breathing to be natural.
Start by saying 'Today I am not going to escape from here into my mind, instead I will be more present here.'
Pick an object to look at, feel your spine as you do.
Now ask yourself 'Am I daydreaming in a way that is receiving guidance or helping me integrate emotional experiences, or am I escaping?'
Then say 'Please help me, if I am receiving guidance, to see what action I need to take, if I am escaping, please help me be present and show me what I am escaping.'

If whenever you stop, you escape into sleepiness and diffuse states, work on increasing your alertness instead of relaxing, keep your eyes open, work on doing something with your hands, doing it for a while, and then deliberately stopping it and noticing what comes afterwards without escaping into your mind.

For example say to yourself 'While you keep your eyes open, press your thumb and forefinger together and let go again a few times. Each time do it more clearly and in a more alert state. Now deliberately stop doing it and notice what happens in the first second after you do, do you feel an echo, or can you feel nothing?' Stay upright while you work at this level.

old: The Milton Model concerns the architecture of the sentence. Commands such as “Relax now,” “Stop being anxious,” or “Trust me” often make a part brace.
Part of the point of indirect language is to get past that reflexive skeptical argument without having to overpower it. The destination can still be deliberate even when the route is subtle.
Begin with what is already true, lower the pressure, presume only a small safe capacity, and invite one movement:
“As the body notices the bed beneath it, it may become a little easier to stop holding the whole day alone.”
Pace reality. Open awareness. Validate function. Presuppose capacity. Bridge gently. Invite one small movement. Test with the body.
new: To do this we are going to use a model that’s called the Milton model. It’s all to do with sentence architecture. When we tell ourselves to ‘be better’, ‘relax now’, ‘stop feeling anxious’ or ‘trust me’ it doesn’t work, does it?
What we need to do is find a way of going around the part that wants to argue with us, so that we can actually get to where we want to get to.
So let’s start with something we know to be true, let’s take the pressure off, presume that we can only do a tiny bit and let’s invite one thing:
‘As my body begins to notice the sensation of the bed underneath it, it may be possible for it to begin to realise that it is not alone in carrying the burden of the day.’

We paced it; we opened up awareness; we validated the reason for the reaction; we presumed we could do it; we used a bridge word to make it easier and we invited one thing. We can then test this out with the body to see if it was possible.

old: Pacing and leading means stating what is already true before inviting anything new.
“Anxiety is here. The body is activated. A protector is trying to help. And one breath at a time, the adult can start to listen.”
The simplest form is a Truth + Invite loop:

“It is completely true that [current sensation or emotion] is here. It makes sense that my system is reacting by [current protective behavior or thought]. And right alongside that truth, my adult self is here, breathing in this room, ready to listen to whatever comes up next.”
new: So how might we pace and lead in a way that works with anxiety?

It might go something like this: ‘It is completely true that the sensation of ________ (or the emotion of _____) is coming up for me. It makes complete sense that my system is trying to react and respond to that by wanting to do or think ________. Whilst that is completely true, there is another thing that is equally true, which is that my adult self is here, breathing in the room right now, and wanting to listen to what comes up for me next.’
Truth, Invite, Truth, Invite etc. is all you need to do.

old: Awareness verbs point attention without yelling at it: notice, realize, recognize, sense, feel, wonder, imagine, picture, listen, allow, discover, remember, consider.
“Notice whether the answer comes as an image, a word, a pressure, a warmth, a silence, or a next action.”
new: Open up awareness by using ‘awareness’ verbs e.g. notice, realise, recognise, sense, feel, wonder, imagine, picture, listen to, allow, discover, remember, consider etc.
Example: ‘Notice how you find out the answer.’

old: A presupposition hides an assumption inside a sentence. Use that power only to presume choice, timing, capacity, safety, love, and adult leadership. Don’t smuggle in obedience.
“Before any part has to change, it can first become more understood.”
new: Presumption is a powerful thing, so please don’t use it except to presume that we will have the choice of when it will happen, that we will be able to do it, that we are safe, that we are loved and that our adult can lead us.

old: Words such as as, while, because, when, after, before, and which means connect one event to another. Use them carefully. A gentle voice doesn’t make a false causal claim true.
Too strong: “Because I breathe, the trauma leaves.” Better: “As I breathe, the adult self may become present enough to hear one small piece of what the wound needs.”
new: Be very careful here. Bridge words are words like ‘as, whilst, because, when, after, before, which means’ etc. These are words that link events. However, even if you say them in a lovely gentle voice it doesn’t mean that it’s true if it isn’t!

In general, the problem with the first example is that it’s too strong. It’s not very likely that just by breathing in and out that your trauma is going to go away! The second example is a lot better as it’s more true.

old: An embedded invitation places a small direction inside a larger sentence. It should invite a modest inner movement, not hide a demand.
“And somewhere inside this breath, I can let the adult self listen.”
“As I sit here, I may allow one small truth to become clear.”
“The child does not have to trust me all at once; it can simply notice I am still here.”
Use one when it helps. Ten embedded invitations in a row feel like somebody took a weekend certification.
new: ie. "And I can allow myself to experience..."
or, "As I sit here, I may begin to allow myself to become aware..."
Or, something similar that you might use when working with "inner child" type of parts.
You can use this, of course, but don't use ten of them one after the other! People will know that you've just come out of some weekend certification course and they won't feel so safe with you.

old: A manipulative double bind traps every answer inside the speaker’s agenda. An ethical one offers two genuinely safe routes.
“Would this part prefer warmth first, or space first?”
new: Manipulative Double Bind Questions are like:
Ethical Double Bind Questions might be:
"Would you prefer to allow a feeling of warmth to come over you now, or would you prefer a feeling of space?"

old: These are questions whose ordinary conversational form also acts as an invitation.
“Can the system show me the next step without showing me the whole wound?”
new: An example of a Conversational Postulate is:
"Can I allow the system to show me the next thing to do, without showing me all the details of wounding that are involved?"

old: Tag questions—isn’t it, can’t it, doesn’t it—can soften a sentence. They become oily very quickly, don’t they? Use them lightly.
“The body already knows something about resting, doesn’t it?”
new: Similarly, you can use 'tag' questions, like "isn't it?" or "can't it?" or "doesn't it?" or others, but be aware that these can get pretty 'oily' pretty quickly, so don't overdo it.
"Your body knows how to relax, doesn't it?"

old: Nominalizations turn processes into nouns: healing, safety, trust, integration, communion, clarity, rest. Their vagueness can sometimes help because the subconscious supplies its own concrete meaning.
“A little more safety can arrive in whatever way the body understands.”
new: Nominalizations are words like, 'healing', 'safety', 'trust', 'integration', 'communion', 'clarity', 'rest', etc. These are a bit vague, and sometimes that can be useful, because it allows the subconscious to fill in the blank with something very specific for that person.
"I can allow myself some safety, in whatever way my body knows how."

old: The Milton Model opens possibility. The Meta Model asks exactly what somebody means. Ethical practice needs both.
“How specifically?” “According to whom?” “Compared to what?” “Always?” “Never?” “What exactly would happen?” “How do I know?” “What evidence would change my mind?”
Use Milton Model to soften into the body. Use Meta Model to return to truth.
new: To 'Milton Model' is to open things up. To 'Meta Model' is to say "What do yo mean by that?" In order to be ethical with people, you need to do both.

"What do you mean specifically? According to who? Compared to what? Always? Never? What specifically would happen if you did? How do you know that? What evidence could you have that would change your mind?"
When people are starting to get stiff in their bodies, 'Milton' it. When you feel like you're losing touch with the truth of what's going on, 'Meta' it.

old: Fear, craving, fantasy, belief, and memory may have sensory qualities: near or far, bright or dim, loud or quiet, moving or still, heavy or light, inside or outside the body. Work with qualities you actually notice. If none are apparent, skip this tool rather than inventing an image or voice.
Ask how the experience is represented. What changes when the image moves two feet back, the voice gets quieter, or the edge becomes less sharp?
“I am not deleting the signal. I am adjusting the volume so I can listen without being overwhelmed.”
Before moving one imaginary pixel, ask the guard whether that change is acceptable.
“Would it be okay if we moved this image back just a little, or lowered the volume slightly, purely so my adult self can stay present enough to hear what you need to tell me?”
new: If someone's fear, craving, fantasy, belief, memory, whatever, has sensory properties in your experience (it has a place in your visual field, or sounds a certain way, or is heavy, or moving, or inside / outside your body, or something like that), you can work with those properties. If there are no sensory properties that you can notice, don't try to create any -- just don't use this tool!
How is this represented for you? Can you allow yourself to move that image back a couple of feet? Can you soften the edges of that image? Can you turn the volume down on that voice in your head? Etc.
"And I can allow myself to know that I am not deleting the message, just turning down the volume so that I am able to be present enough to hear what it is."
And, always ask the guard if it's ok to do this.
"Is it ok to move that image back a couple of feet and turn the volume down a bit, so that I can be present enough to hear what you need me to hear?"
